source_review.notes: Checked current Linux kernel documentation for self-protection, KASAN, KMSAN, KFENCE, UBSAN, KCSAN, refcount_t, Rust support and unsafe-code guidance, and AArch64 MTE, plus current Clang KCFI documentation. All eleven official URLs returned HTTP 200 after normal redirects. Prevention, dynamic detection, sampling, probabilistic tagging, exploitation hardening and empirical assurance claims remain explicitly distinct.

evidence: Checked handle, offset, length, operation, time, capacity, birth, death, permission, synchronization, generation and tag-space notation.
Reviewed conjunction, lifetime interval, subtraction-based range bound and simplified independent tag-miss probability.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Notation separates object denotation, temporal validity, spatial validity, authority, synchronization and probabilistic detection.

evidence: Executed 32-bit wrapped addition for capacity 4096, offset 0xfffffff0 and length 64 and confirmed the wrapped end is 48.
Confirmed the naive wrapped-sum test accepts, the subtraction-based check rejects, and an ordinary offset 4000 length 64 range is accepted.
numerical_recomputation.notes: The deterministic computation validates fixed-width wrap and two range predicates only; Python code does not model kernel pointers, objects, concurrency or hardware accesses.

evidence: Re-derived valid access as denotation plus lifetime, bounds, operation permission and synchronization obligations.

Verified that evaluating offset at most capacity before length at most capacity minus offset avoids representing an overflowing endpoint; derived q^-k only under stated independent uniform re-tag assumptions.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The tag model is deliberately simplified and excludes finite allocator policy, granules, retained tags, reuse correlations and asynchronous fault behavior.

evidence: Reviewed zero and huge lengths, wrapped counts, flexible layouts, partial construction, stale handles, refcount acquisition races, RCU readers and asynchronous callbacks.
Reviewed user remapping, MMIO, DMA teardown, unsound safe wrappers, instrumentation gaps, tag collisions, sampled allocations, release-only behavior and recovery after corruption.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: Representation, lifecycle, concurrency, language, user/device, detector, hardware, deployment and incident boundaries receive separate treatment.

evidence: Traced allocation, semantic initialization, publication, access, reference transfer, revocation, grace period, destruction, DMA unmap and reuse.
Mapped prevention, sanitizers, sampling, tag checks, allocator defenses, permissions and CFI to their precise coverage and blind spots.
invariant_checking.notes: The invariant set preserves object identity, range, lifetime, ownership, synchronization and evidence labeling across the full lifecycle.

evidence: Reviewed twelve representation, construction, denotation, bounds, ownership, concurrency, boundary, detection, hardening, remediation, recovery and claim obligations.
Constructed counterexamples for non-null-as-valid, lock-as-owner, zero-as-initialized, safe-language-as-universal, sanitizer-clean-as-proof, tagging-as-deterministic and CFI-as-memory-safety claims.
proof_review.notes: The chapter supplies reusable object-lifecycle proof obligations, not a formal proof of C, Rust, Linux, a compiler, sanitizer, allocator, architecture or kernel configuration.

evidence: Audited uses of safe, valid, live, owned, initialized, instrumented, detected, sampled, hardened, protected, prevented and recovered.
Confirmed that safe abstractions depend on sound unsafe internals, detectors cover executions, tags can collide, and exploitation defenses do not remove underlying corruption.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: Language guarantees, API invariants, dynamic observations, probability models, operational recommendations and assurance limits remain separately labeled.

evidence: artifacts/snippets/OS-094/report.json records source, expected and actual output, stderr, exit status, Python toolchain and environment for overflow-safe range validation.
Reviewed required compiler, kernel config, architecture, sanitizer mode, exclusions, workload, allocator/reference history, crash, DMA, performance and fix evidence.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: The passing toy establishes four integer/predicate outputs only; it provides no evidence for a real kernel access, C undefined behavior, Rust soundness, sanitizer coverage, MTE, KFENCE, DMA ownership or exploit resistance.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed kernel memory safety as object identity, range, lifetime, initialization, permission and synchronization across allocation-to-reuse, with prevention, detection and hardening as distinct layers.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed implementable concerns including checked arithmetic, user copies, DMA, refcounts, RCU, safe Rust boundaries, C APIs, sanitizers, fuzzing, tagging, allocator and control-flow hardening, configuration matrices, triage and recovery. Internal practitioner-oriented review only.

pedagogical_review.notes: Verified progression from fault taxonomy and lifecycle through language and API prevention to dynamic detection, hardware and exploitation defenses, evidence and remediation, followed by twelve obligations, sixteen trade-offs, twenty-six misconceptions, ten examples and five complete exercises.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external operating-systems academic, Linux memory-management or Rust-for-Linux maintainer, compiler or sanitizer engineer, hardware-architecture expert, kernel security reviewer, independent-verification or certification review is claimed.
